config.framing_prompt: The German federal minimum wage currently stands at €12.82 per hour, set by the independent Mindestlohnkommission. Several parties have proposed raising it to €15 per hour by 2026, while others argue the commission's independence must not be overridden by political targets. Discuss whether the minimum wage should be raised to €15, considering the effects on low-wage workers, small and medium-sized businesses, and regional economic differences between western and eastern Germany. Ground your arguments in your party's documented positions.

turns.text: Regarding the SPD's argument that raising the minimum wage to €15 per hour would significantly improve the living standards of low-wage workers, we must carefully consider the potential consequences for our Mittelstand, which is the backbone of the German economy. Raising the minimum wage too sharply could lead to increased labor costs, potentially harming the competitiveness of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This might force them to reduce their workforce or even go out of business, ultimately harming the very workers the SPD aims to protect. We should trust the independent Mindestlohnkommission to assess the economic conditions and adjust the minimum wage accordingly, rather than imposing a one-size-fits-all solution.

As outlined in our party's programme, we support a "good work" culture that prioritizes dignity and security for all workers, regardless of their employer's size. A €15 minimum wage is a crucial step towards achieving this vision.

turns.text: Regarding the CDU/CSU's argument that the independent Mindestlohnkommission should assess the economic conditions and adjust the minimum wage accordingly, we fundamentally disagree with the notion that the commission's independence must come at the expense of a living wage for all workers. As we emphasize in our party's programme, a "good work" culture requires a fair minimum wage that allows workers to cover their basic needs and participate in the economy. The current €12.82 minimum wage is already too low, and the commission has failed to catch up with the rising cost of living. By 2026, Germany's GDP per capita is expected to exceed €45,000, yet our minimum wage has not kept pace with economic growth. It's time to rethink the commission's role and prioritize the needs of low-wage workers. Raising the minimum wage to €15 per hour would be a crucial step towards a more equitable and sustainable economy.
